key_results: The signals-and-systems abstraction characterizes a physical, mathematical, or computational object solely by how it maps an input signal to an output. Because the representation suppresses substrate details, the same form is widely applicable, modular, and hierarchical. [Session 1, slides 7–14]

Sampling forms a DT sequence x[n]=x(nT) from a CT signal; reconstruction maps samples back to CT, with zero-order hold and piecewise-linear interpolation presented as two distinct practical rules. [Session 1, slides 15–18]

For the linear leaky tank, conservation plus outflow proportional to height gives dr1/dt=(r0−r1)/τ. The constant τ has units of time and determines the exponential approach to steady state. [Session 1, slides 25–35]

DT systems are deliberately represented four ways: a verbal rationale, a compact difference equation, a signal-flow block diagram, and an operator expression. Equations state constraints, while block diagrams also specify an executable signal-flow interpretation and input/output roles. [Session 2, slides 3–21]

With R denoting one unit of right shift, a DT realization made from adders, gains, and delays can be manipulated as a polynomial or rational expression in R. Cascades multiply operator expressions, and distributive/associative/commutative algebra reveals equivalent realizations when systems start at rest. [Session 2, slides 22–35]

The accumulator obeys (1−R)Y=X and has functional 1/(1−R)=1+R+R²+…, so a one-sample transient produces a persistent unit-step response. Feedback appears as a cyclic signal path, and each traversal adds another output sample. [Session 2, slides 36–47]

An acyclic finite add/gain/delay network has a finite-duration impulse response, whereas a cyclic network can have an infinite-duration response. A single loop of gain p produces the fundamental mode p^n u[n], converging for |p|<1 and diverging for |p|>1. [Session 2, slides 43–56; Session 3, slides 5–12]

Higher-order rational DT systems factor into first-order pole factors. Partial fractions rewrite their impulse responses as weighted sums of geometric fundamental modes and yield equivalent cascade or parallel realizations. [Session 3, slides 13–23]

DT poles are the roots of the denominator after substituting R→1/z. Real poles control monotone or alternating geometric growth; complex-conjugate poles re^{±jΩ} produce real damped or growing oscillations whose envelope is r^n and angular frequency is Ω. [Session 3, slides 9–27 and 39–44]

The Fibonacci recurrence has poles φ=(1+√5)/2 and −1/φ; its impulse response is a weighted sum of the divergent φ^n mode and alternating decaying (−1/φ)^n mode, giving a nonrecursive closed form for Fibonacci numbers. [Session 3, slides 28–38]

For CT systems, the operator A integrates from −∞ to the present: Y=AX means y(t)=∫_{−∞}^t x(τ)dτ. Replacing DT delays by CT integrators creates a parallel operator calculus for linear constant-coefficient differential equations. [Session 4, slides 2–10]

The CT impulse δ(t) is introduced as the limit of unit-area pulses whose width tends to zero. It is nonzero only at zero yet integrates to one, and its integral is the unit step u(t). [Session 4, slides 14–18]

The one-integrator feedback system ẏ=x+py has system functional A/(1−pA) and impulse response e^{pt}u(t). Each loop traversal adds an integration, building the exponential Taylor series; CT convergence requires Re(p)<0. [Session 4, slides 20–35]

The undamped mass–spring system has conjugate poles s=±j√(K/M). Real inputs excite conjugate mode pairs whose imaginary parts cancel; its impulse response is ω0 sin(ω0t)u(t), with ω0=√(K/M). [Session 4, slides 41–48]

The bilateral Z transform is X(z)=Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞}x[n]z^{−n}. The transform is not fully specified by its rational expression: its region of convergence is essential and encodes whether pole contributions are right-sided or left-sided. [Session 5, slides 14–21 and 25–42]

A right-sided α^n u[n] and the corresponding left-sided −α^n u[−1−n] both have rational form z/(z−α), but their ROCs are |z|>|α| and |z|<|α| respectively. Multiple poles partition the z-plane into candidate annular ROCs. [Session 5, slides 25–38]

For a linear constant-coefficient difference equation, taking Z transforms and using x[n−1]↔z^{−1}X(z) converts the recurrence into algebra; H(z)=Y(z)/X(z) is a ratio of polynomials whose numerator and denominator roots are zeros and poles. [Session 5, slides 22–25 and 43]

Core Z-transform properties in this shard are linearity, delay, multiplication by n (nx[n]↔−z dX/dz), and convolution (x1*x2↔X1X2), with ROCs at least as large as the stated intersections subject to cancellation. [Session 5, slides 22–23 and 44–50]

For a rational DT LTI system, causality corresponds to a right-sided impulse response and an ROC outside the outermost pole; stability requires the ROC to include the unit circle. A causal rational system is stable when all uncancelled poles lie inside the unit circle. [Problem Set 3, Problem 5 and solution]

The bilateral Laplace transform X(s)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(t)e^{−st}dt maps CT signals to functions of complex s. Right-sided signals have right-half-plane ROCs, left-sided signals have left-half-plane ROCs, and two-sided signals can have a vertical-strip ROC. [Session 6, slides 7–24]

The same rational Laplace expression can describe distinct left-, right-, or two-sided time functions depending on ROC. For example, e^{−|t|} transforms to 2/(1−s²) only on −1<Re(s)<1. [Session 6, slides 12–24]

Under the bilateral transform, d x(t)/dt↔sX(s) when boundary terms vanish, and δ(t)↔1 by the sifting property. Linear constant-coefficient differential equations therefore become algebraic equations without separately constructing homogeneous and particular solutions. [Session 6, slides 25–33]

Core Laplace properties in the shard are linearity, delay, multiplication by t, exponential weighting, time differentiation/integration, and convolution. The convolution integral maps to the product X1(s)X2(s). [Session 6, slide 34]

For a right-sided signal with no impulse or higher singularity at zero, the initial-value theorem gives x(0+)=lim_{s→∞}sX(s). If the signal has a finite asymptotic limit, the final-value theorem gives x(∞)=lim_{s→0}sX(s); the limit/existence conditions matter. [Session 6, slides 35–36; Problem Set 4, Problem 4]

Forward Euler replaces an integrator by TR/(1−R), producing the pole map z=1+sT. It preserves CT stability only for poles inside the circle of radius 1/T centered at −1/T; for the leaky tank, stability requires T/τ<2. [Session 7, slides 9–20]

Backward Euler replaces an integrator by T/(1−R), producing z=1/(1−sT). It maps the entire open left half of the s-plane into the z-plane disk of radius 1/2 centered at 1/2, so every stable CT pole remains stable after discretization. [Session 7, slides 21–31]

The trapezoidal rule gives A→(T/2)(z+1)/(z−1), or z=(1+sT/2)/(1−sT/2). It maps the left half-plane inside the unit circle and maps the jω axis exactly onto the unit circle, avoiding artificial growth or decay of undamped modes. [Session 7, slides 32–38]

Linearity means weighted input sums produce the same weighted output sums; time invariance means shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount. Together they let any signal be decomposed into weighted shifted impulses whose responses superpose. [Session 8, slides 15–21]

For a DT LTI system, the impulse response h[n] completely determines the system and y[n]=(x*h)[n]=Σ_k x[k]h[n−k]. Convolution acts on whole signals, despite the conventional shorthand x[n]*h[n]. [Session 8, slides 21–42]
The CT counterpart is y(t)=(x*h)(t)=∫_{−∞}^{∞}x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ, obtained by taking the limit of a weighted train of narrow pulses. [Session 8, slides 43–48]

Optical blurring can be modeled as convolution with a point-spread function: a microscope’s three-dimensional impulse response directly measures blur across and along its optical axis, while a ground telescope combines atmospheric and diffraction point-spread functions. [Session 8, slides 50–65]

Repeated poles generate polynomial-weighted modes rather than ordinary weighted sums of distinct geometrics: a double pole at z=1 yields h[n]=(n+1)u[n] and can be realized as two cascaded accumulators. [Problem Set 2, Problem 7 and solution]

Substituting every delay R by R^m maps each original pole to all mth roots of that pole. Substituting R/2 instead halves pole locations; roots of poles inside the unit circle remain inside, preserving stability under the delay-expansion construction. [Problem Set 3, Problem 7 and solution]

The impedance method is exactly the Laplace transform of circuit laws: KCL, KVL, and resistor relations retain their algebraic form, while inductors and capacitors acquire impedances sL and 1/(sC). [Problem Set 4, Problem 6 and solution]

The Fall 2011 Quiz 1 checks that the first seven sessions can be traversed in both directions: waveform→recurrence coefficients, impulse-response shape→poles/zeros, time signal→Laplace transform and ROC, and coupled ODEs→partial-fraction system function. [Quiz 1, Problems 1–4]
pedagogy: A representation-first, active-learning course sequence. Each lecture repeatedly translates one system among a physical story, differential/difference equation, block diagram, operator functional, impulse response, transform, and pole–zero picture; concept-map slides make those translations explicit. Short ‘Check Yourself’ multiple-choice sequences first elicit a prediction, then reveal a worked answer, while animations in the slide deck trace samples through feedback loops or flip/shift convolution step by step. Physical cases—leaky tanks, capacitors, drug clearance, masses and springs, microscopes, and Hubble—arrive before or alongside abstraction. The four problem sets contain 29 multi-part problems: concise exam-style exercises plus larger ‘Engineering Design Problems’ requiring modeling, Python/Matlab experiments, plots, numerical-versus-analytic comparisons, or circuit derivations. Full solutions explain alternative approaches and common conceptual distinctions. Homework 4 is explicitly optional exam practice; Quiz 1 has four equally weighted synthesis problems. The course assumes calculus, ordinary differential equations, complex arithmetic/Euler’s identity, elementary circuits and mechanics, and enough Python or Matlab to simulate recurrences; it develops transforms, pole reasoning, and convolution from that base. Lecture 2’s correction workflow also treats reading solutions and marking one’s own errors as part of learning, not merely grading.

gems: The opening cell-phone example turns a long acoustic–electrical–radio–optical–radio–acoustic chain into one system block, demonstrating abstraction, modularity, and hierarchy before any transform algebra appears. [Session 1, slides 10–13]

The leaky tank’s time constant is made physical: with equal outlet holes, a wider tank changes height more slowly, and the same conservation equation becomes a capacitor model by replacing accumulated water with charge. [Session 1, slides 25–36]

A difference machine is motivated as compression: store the first large value, then only successive differences when neighboring values are nearly equal. The same idea is immediately shown as words, equation, diagram, and operator. [Session 2, slides 4–22]

The accumulator is the first memorable feedback surprise: one impulse enters, but the output remains one forever—‘persistent response to a transient input’—because every loop traversal writes another sample. [Session 2, slides 37–47]

Fibonacci’s rabbit recurrence becomes a pole calculation: φ and −1/φ reveal one growing and one alternating decaying mode, then combine into a closed form that computes f[n] without f[n−1] or f[n−2]. [Session 3, slides 28–38]

A real six-sample oscillation emerges from poles e^{±jπ/3}; the impulse response 1,1,0,−1,−1,0,… connects recurrence, unit-circle geometry, partial fractions, and periodicity in one compact example. [Session 3, slides 39–42; Problem Set 3, Problem 6]

The CT impulse is introduced through apparently contradictory requirements—nonzero only at one instant but unit total area—resolved by a family of ever narrower unit-area pulses. [Session 4, slides 15–18]

Repeated CT integrations around a feedback loop literally assemble the Taylor series 1+pt+p²t²/2!+…, making e^{pt} a visible consequence of the block diagram rather than a guessed ODE solution. [Session 4, slides 20–35]
One rational Z expression z/(z−7/8) describes either a causal decaying sequence or a noncausal left-sided growing sequence; only the shaded ROC tells which signal was meant. [Session 5, slides 25–33]

The two-sided signal e^{−|t|} produces the vertical-strip ROC −1<Re(s)<1, a particularly clean demonstration that an ROC is the overlap of convergence demands from the two time directions. [Session 6, slides 14–17]

Problem Set 1’s two-tank design goes from conservation laws to a second-order ODE, a cascade interpretation, and a forward-Euler simulation. For T=1 s the one-tank analytic/numerical discrepancy stays below 0.00094 over the tested 60 s. [Problem Set 1, Problem 6 and solution]

The drug-dosing model explains a loading dose with one line of feedback: daily unit doses approach 1/(1−α), so choosing the first dose as 1/(1−α) places the blood level at steady state from day zero. [Problem Set 1, Problem 7 and solution]

An undamped mass–spring is a numerical stress test: forward Euler invents growing oscillations, backward Euler invents damping, and the centered rule closely follows the exact 1−cos t step response. [Problem Set 2, Problem 8 and solution; Session 7]

Approximating a double pole by two nearby simple poles explains both convergence and numerical danger: as ε shrinks from 0.1 to 0.001, two terms of magnitude about 500 cancel to produce values near 1,2,3,… . [Problem Set 2, Problem 7d–e and solution]
The complex-number warm-up j^j=e^{−π/2} is real, because writing j=e^{jπ/2} turns a seemingly exotic power into a decaying exponential. [Problem Set 3, Problem 1a and solution]
The complex geometric-sum design problem turns Σ_{n=0}^{100}(0.8+0.2j)^n into a shrinking spiral and predicts its endpoint near 1/(0.2−0.2j)=(5/√2)e^{jπ/4}. [Problem Set 3, Problem 8 and solution]
A finite triangular pulse is decoded from (1−e^{−s})²/s² as three delayed ramps: +1 slope at t=0, −2 at t=1, and +1 at t=2. [Problem Set 4, Problem 2d and solution]

The impedance-method problem derives a second-order RLC equation by KCL/KVL, then obtains the identical system function by replacing resistor values in an ordinary divider with sL and 1/(sC). [Problem Set 4, Problem 6 and solution]

The microscope resolves a 0.09 μm calibration bead as an approximately 0.53 μm-wide spot and shows still greater blur along the optical axis, making the 3D impulse response an experimentally measurable system signature. [Session 8, slides 58–62]

Hubble’s first star images reveal a mirror ground just 2.2 μm too flat; COSTAR is introduced as ‘eyeglasses for Hubble,’ followed by before/after observations that turn point-spread-function theory into a historical engineering rescue. [Session 8, slides 68–73]
Quiz 1’s impulse-train problem links a CT train of unit impulses at integer times to the geometric series Σe^{−sn}=1/(1−e^{−s}), with ROC Re(s)>0. [Quiz 1, Problem 3b and solution]
